title: Numbers, prices, and haggling
goal: Read numbers into the tens of thousands, ask prices, say amounts of money the spoken and the written way, and haggle without feeling awkward.
bekal: ask the price with 多少钱 and the quantity with 几
say prices with 块, 毛, 分
buy something from hello to change
haggle with 便宜一点儿吧

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — At the fruit stall
dialogs.intro: Andi is shopping at the market near his home. Notice that the seller says 块, not 元 — that's the form you actually hear every day.

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Hello! What can I get you?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Excuse me, how much are the apples per jin?
lines.literal: please — ask, apple — how-much — money — one — jin.

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Eight fifty a jin. Really sweet!
lines.literal: eight — yuan — five, one — jin. (support) — sweet.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: That's a bit pricey. Could you go a little lower?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: All right, eight. How many jin would you like?
lines.literal: good — (suggestion), eight — yuan. you(polite) — want — how-many — jin.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Two jin. What about the bananas?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Bananas are six. That's twenty-two altogether.
lines.literal: banana — six — yuan. altogether — twenty-two — yuan.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Here's a hundred.

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Seventy-eight is your change. Thank you!

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Thank you! Goodbye!

notes: **[多少钱|Duōshao qián]？ = how much is it?** Literally “how much money”. To add the unit, put it after: [多少钱一斤|duōshao qián yì jīn] how much per jin, [多少钱一个|duōshao qián yí ge] how much each.

**⚠️ [几|jǐ] and [多少|duōshao] both mean “how many”, but they aren't interchangeable.** 几 is for amounts **expected to be under ten** and **must be followed by a measure word**: [几个人|jǐ ge rén], [几点|jǐ diǎn]. 多少 is for large or unknown amounts, **with no measure word needed**: [多少钱|duōshao qián], [多少人|duōshao rén].
**[块|kuài] is the word people actually say** for Chinese money. [元|yuán] is only written — on price tags, receipts, and at the bank. Say 八元 at a market and you'll instantly sound like a textbook.
**Prices with decimals: [八块五|bā kuài wǔ] = 8.50 yuan.** The last part can stand bare, without 毛. The full form is [八块五毛|bā kuài wǔ máo], but people rarely say it all.

**[有点儿|yǒudiǎnr] + adjective = “a bit …”, and it always sounds negative.** [有点儿贵|yǒudiǎnr guì] a bit expensive, [有点儿累|yǒudiǎnr lèi] a bit tired. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with [一点儿|yìdiǎnr], which comes **after** the adjective and means “a little more”: [便宜一点儿|piányi yìdiǎnr] = a little cheaper.
**[吧|ba] at the end of a sentence softens a request.** [便宜一点儿吧|Piányi yìdiǎnr ba] sounds like a suggestion, not a demand. This one syllable changes the whole feel of your sentence.
**[找|zhǎo] means “look for”, but at the till it means “give change”.** [找您七十八块|Zhǎo nín qīshíbā kuài] = your change is 78 yuan.
**[斤|jīn] is a Chinese unit of weight = 500 grams**, not a kilogram (about 1.1 pounds). Market prices are almost always given per 斤, so a price that sounds cheap is actually double per kilo.

grammars.title: Numbers from 0 to 99,999
body: Mandarin numbers are very regular — far more regular than English, with its *eleven*, *twelve*, and *-teens*. After ten, numbers are read exactly as they're built: 11 = 10 + 1, 25 = 2 × 10 + 5.
after: ⚠️ **A zero in the middle must be said.** 101 isn't 一百一 but [一百零一|yìbǎi líng yī]. Skip the zero and 105 and 150 become impossible to tell apart.

⚠️ **Mandarin groups numbers every FOUR digits, not three.** After [千|qiān] (1,000) comes not “ten thousand” but a new unit: [万|wàn] = 10,000. So 250,000 is read as 25 万 — [二十五万|èrshíwǔ wàn]. This is the biggest source of confusion for English speakers hearing large prices. Practice: read ten electronics prices out loud today.
⚠️ **两 vs 二 once more**: [两百|liǎngbǎi] 200 and [两千|liǎngqiān] 2,000 use 两, but [二十|èrshí] 20 uses 二. The rule: 两 is used when the two **multiplies** a big unit.

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — Buying clothes and haggling
dialogs.intro: Haggling is a normal part of shopping at Chinese markets — not in big stores or supermarkets. Notice that Andi is never rude; he just holds his ground calmly.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How much is this top?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Three hundred eighty. It's good quality.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: That's way too expensive! Can you go a bit lower?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: How much do you want to pay?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How about two hundred?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Two hundred is too little. Let's say three hundred.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Two fifty. OK?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: All right, two fifty. What color do you want?
lines.literal: good — (suggestion), two-hundred — five. want — what — color.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: The blue one. Can I try it on?

lines.speaker: 老板:
lines.id: Of course. The fitting room is over there.

notes: **[太贵了|Tài guì le]！** — the first sentence out of your mouth when haggling. The pattern [太|tài] + adjective + [了|le] means “too …”, and the 了 at the end is almost never dropped.
**[怎么样|zěnmeyàng]？ = “how about it?”** — used to offer an opinion or a suggestion. [两百怎么样|Liǎngbǎi zěnmeyàng]？ = how about two hundred? This is the gentlest way to haggle.
**[两百五|liǎngbǎi wǔ] = 250, not 205.** When the last digit stands alone at the end of a price, it fills **the next place down**. For 205 you must say [两百零五|liǎngbǎi líng wǔ] with 零.

**[试试|shìshi] = “give it a try”.** Doubling a verb makes the action sound light and brief — like “have a quick …” in English. [看看|kànkan] have a look, [听听|tīngting] have a listen, [想想|xiǎngxiang] think it over.
**[当然|dāngrán] = of course.** A word that makes your answer sound friendly, not just agreeable.
⚠️ **Haggling is only normal at markets, street stalls, and small shops.** In supermarkets, chain stores, and restaurants, haggling is considered odd — much as it would be at home.

grammars.title: Two ways to say “a bit” and “a little”
body: This is the pair learners mix up most, and the mistake is instantly audible. The difference is **where it stands**.

rows: [请说慢一点儿|Qǐng shuō màn yìdiǎnr]。

after: How to remember it: **有点儿 comes before a complaint, 一点儿 trails after a request.** If your sentence expresses a wish for something to change, use 一点儿.

sections.title: Surviving at the checkout and in shops

blocks.text: Sellers say the same sentences every day. You don't need to be able to say them — you just need to **recognize** them and know the short reply.

blocks.title: Paying by phone
items: Cash has nearly vanished from China's big cities. Two words you must recognize: **[微信|Wēixìn]** (WeChat Pay) and **[支付宝|Zhīfùbǎo]** (Alipay).
[可以用微信吗|Kěyǐ yòng Wēixìn ma]？ — Can I use WeChat?
[扫这个|Sǎo zhège]。 — “Scan this one.” 扫 = scan a QR code.
[我没有中国的手机号|Wǒ méiyǒu Zhōngguó de shǒujī hào]。 — “I don't have a Chinese phone number.” A sentence you'll need often as a newcomer.

blocks.title: Numbers in everyday life
items: **Phone and room numbers are read digit by digit**, and 1 is read [幺|yāo] so it isn't confused with 七. The number 138-1174 is read *yāo sān bā, yāo yāo qī sì*.
**The number 4** ([四|sì]) is avoided because it sounds like [死|sǐ] “die”. Many buildings have no 4th, 14th, or 24th floor.
**The number 8** ([八|bā]) is loved because it sounds like [发|fā] “prosper”. Phone numbers full of 8s sell for high prices.

**Discounts are read the opposite way from English.** [打八折|dǎ bā zhé] isn't 80% off but **pay 80%**, i.e. 20% off. [打五折|dǎ wǔ zhé] = 50% off. ⚠️ Misreading this can make you think something is four times cheaper than it really is.
